q: Explain the argument for and against Oregon's 90% varietal rule.
accept: purity of expression versus blending flexibility marketing integrity
integrity versus flexibility
ans: For: it guarantees varietal integrity and built Oregon's reputation. Against: it denies blending flexibility in difficult vintages that federal law would permit
exp: Regulatory trade-off questions test judgement, not recall.

q: Explain Ontario's appellation structure below the provincial level.
accept: niagara peninsula regional appellations sub-appellations beamsville bench twenty mile
niagara sub-appellations
~designated viticultural areas
~designated viticultural area
ans: Below the provincial 'Ontario' appellation sit the Designated Viticultural Areas — Niagara Peninsula, Lake Erie North Shore and Prince Edward County. Only Niagara Peninsula subdivides further: into regional appellations (Niagara Escarpment, Niagara-on-the-Lake) and then ten sub-appellations, among them Beamsville Bench, Twenty Mile Bench, Short Hills Bench, Creek Shores, Four Mile Creek and St. David's Bench
exp: A Burgundian nesting on a Canadian map.

q: The Columbia Gorge AVA sells itself as 'a world of wine in forty miles'. Explain what makes that literally true.
accept: the cascade gap and rain shadow give a rainfall gradient across forty miles
wet cool west end to dry warm east end inside one appellation
the gorge cuts the cascades so rainfall drops sharply eastward
marine air through the gorge then rain shadow cool to warm gradient
forty miles takes you from forty inches of rain to under ten
ans: The Gorge is the only near-sea-level breach in the Cascade Range, so marine air pours inland through it and then the rain shadow rebuilds as you move east. The AVA runs about forty miles along both banks of the Columbia, in Oregon and Washington alike, from roughly 35–40 inches of annual rainfall at the western end to under 10 at the eastern. West end, cool and damp: Pinot Noir, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Gris. East end, warm and dry: Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Tempranillo. One appellation containing a full cool-to-warm gradient, because the mountain gap and the rain shadow are compressed into a very short run.
exp: Established in 2004 and deliberately drawn across the state line, the Gorge is one of the few AVAs whose identity is a gradient rather than a style — and its eastern portion overlaps the Columbia Valley AVA, so a grower there may label either way. Set it against its neighbours to show you understand what an AVA can be founded on: the Rocks District is defined by a single soil series, Red Mountain by heat and aspect, the Gorge by change itself. It is also the mechanism behind Washington's entire east-side climate, since the same gap and the same Cascade shadow are what make the Columbia Basin a desert.

q: Compare the Finger Lakes and Long Island as growing environments, and explain what each plants as a result.
accept: finger lakes fear winter kill and plant riesling long island fears rot and plants merlot
continental winter risk versus maritime growing season risk
the lakes buffer winter cold the atlantic buffers winter but brings humidity
riesling in the finger lakes bordeaux varieties on long island
one region is limited by january the other by september
ans: The Finger Lakes are continental and the danger is winter: mid-winter lows can kill buds and split trunks, so the deep lakes' thermal mass and the near-shore slopes are the whole game, the season is short, and the plantings are Riesling above all, with Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and a surviving hybrid base for insurance. Long Island is maritime and the danger is the growing season: humidity, rot pressure and Atlantic storms in September, but almost no winter kill and one of the East's longest, latest seasons — so it plants Bordeaux, Merlot leading, with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc. Cold-hardiness selects the Finger Lakes' varieties; disease pressure and hang time select Long Island's.
exp: Name the risk before the grape — that is the deductive habit examiners reward, and it generalises to every cold region you will be asked about. The Finger Lakes' hybrids are insurance against a −25°C night, and the region's site selection is entirely about how far from the water and how high on the slope you are. Long Island's canopy work, leaf pulling and spray programme are insurance against a wet September. Both are New York, and blurring them means missing that 'cold climate' and 'cool climate' are different problems requiring opposite solutions.

q: Explain British Columbia's appellation hierarchy and name three Okanagan sub-GIs.
accept: bc vqa then geographical indications then okanagan sub gis golden mile bench naramata bench okanagan falls
golden mile bench was the first sub gi naramata bench and skaha bench followed
okanagan valley is a gi with sub gis such as naramata bench
province then gi then sub gi with golden mile bench first in 2015
the okanagan subdivides into benches like naramata and skaha
ans: BC VQA sits above the province's named Geographical Indications: Okanagan Valley, Similkameen Valley, Vancouver Island, Fraser Valley and Gulf Islands, joined in 2018 by Thompson Valley, Shuswap, Lillooet and Kootenays. Inside the Okanagan sits the third, Burgundian layer — the sub-GIs. Golden Mile Bench was the first, granted in 2015, followed by Okanagan Falls, Naramata Bench, Skaha Bench and Lake Country, with further additions since.
exp: Golden Mile Bench matters chiefly as precedent: it was the first boundary in BC drawn on soil, aspect and elevation rather than on convenience, and it opened the door to the bench-by-bench mapping the valley now has. A Master-level answer should also register how fragile the base is — the January 2024 Arctic event effectively erased that vintage's crop, and the province temporarily allowed wineries to vinify out-of-province fruit, which cannot carry BC VQA. An appellation system is only as strong as the fruit standing behind it.

q: Prince Edward County: name its soil, its grapes, and the winter practice its growers cannot skip.
accept: limestone soil chardonnay and pinot noir and buttage hilling up the vines for winter
thin soil over limestone and burying the vines each winter
buttage means hilling soil over the vines chardonnay and pinot noir on limestone
hilling soil over the graft union to survive winter in prince edward county
the county buries its vines every autumn and uncovers them in spring
ans: A thin cap of soil over Trenton limestone on a peninsula in Lake Ontario — the Ontario region built on a Burgundian argument, planted to Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with Cabernet Franc, Gamay and Riesling behind them. Winters are severe enough that growers practise buttage: in late autumn soil is ploughed up over the graft union and the retained canes so the buried wood survives even if everything exposed is killed, then unearthed — débuttage — in spring. It became a VQA Designated Viticultural Area in 2007.
exp: Buttage is the clearest example in the New World of a region whose economics are set by winter rather than by the market: two extra passes of ploughing a year, vine and trunk damage from the machinery, and shorter vine lifespans, all of which keep the County small and its bottles expensive. It also explains the varietal choice — you will hill up for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir on limestone, but not for a commodity grape. Contrast the Niagara Peninsula, where the escarpment and the lake do that work for the grower.

q: Explain the 1756 Douro demarcation's significance and who ordered it.
accept: marques de pombal first demarcated wine region 1756
pombal companhia geral
ans: The Marquês de Pombal established the Companhia Geral and demarcated the Douro (1756) — among the world's first regulated wine regions
exp: Granite marker posts (feitorias) still stand in the vineyards.

q: Name the three principal Douro terrace systems and their eras.
accept: socalcos patamares vinha ao alto
pre-phylloxera socalcos patamares bulldozed vertical planting
ans: Socalcos (ancient narrow stone terraces), patamares (mechanized bulldozed terraces, 1970s+), vinha ao alto (vertical up-slope rows)
exp: Each trades labor cost against erosion and sun exposure.

q: What is a 'lagar' and why does the Douro still use them?
accept: granite treading tank foot treading extraction fast
shallow granite tanks foot trodden
ans: Shallow granite treading tanks — human feet extract color/tannin gently and fast during Port's short pre-fortification window
exp: Robotic lagares now mimic the pressure and rhythm of a human foot.

q: Give the Douro's aguardente specification for fortifying Port.
accept: 77% neutral grape spirit 115 liters per pipe
aguardente 77 abv
ans: ~77% ABV neutral grape spirit, ~115 L per 550 L pipe, added when roughly half the sugar remains
exp: Contrast VDN's 96% spirit — a favorite comparative question.

q: Which Portuguese region grows 'Baga' and what did Luís Pato name his declassified wines to protest the DOC?
accept: bairrada vinho regional beiras
beiras regional labels
ans: Bairrada; Pato labeled under Vinho Regional Beiras during his dispute with the DOC
exp: His daughter Filipa's 'Post-Quercus' amphora wines continue the family heresy.

q: Name Portugal's white grape most associated with Bucelas and its acidity claim.
accept: arinto
ans: Arinto (Pedernã in Vinho Verde) — acidity that survives heat, hence its spread nationwide
exp: Bucelas was 'Portuguese Hock' to Wellington's officers.

q: Which Azorean and Madeiran vine-training walls protect against Atlantic salt, and what are they called on Pico?
accept: currais lajido basalt corrals
currais stone corrals
ans: Currais — basalt corrals on the lajido lava fields of Pico (UNESCO listed)
exp: Verdelho, Arinto dos Açores, Terrantez do Pico grow inside them.

q: Explain why Douro table wine now competes with Port economically.
accept: beneficio limits port production surplus fruit dry wine higher demand
dry wines absorb excess and demand shifted
ans: Beneficio caps Port production; surplus quality fruit goes to dry wine, and global demand has shifted from fortified to table wine
exp: The Douro Boys built the market the beneficio made inevitable.

q: Explain how a Vintage Port comes to be declared, and the difference between a classic declaration and a single-quinta Vintage.
accept: samples approved by the ivdp in the second year and bottled between the second and third year
houses declare in the second year with single quinta bottlings filling undeclared years
the ivdp approves the declaration a classic is a multi quinta blend a single quinta comes from one property
ans: In the spring of the second year following the harvest, a shipper submits samples and a proposed quantity to the IVDP, which must approve both before the wine may be sold as Vintage; the house then declares publicly, and the trade's houses tend to declare together. Bottling falls between 1 July of the second year and 30 June of the third, so the wine spends roughly two years in cask or vat and does every remaining year of its ageing in bottle — unfiltered, which is why it throws a heavy crust and must be decanted. A classic declaration is the house's blend of its finest quintas in a year good enough for the house to attach its own name; historically that happens around three times a decade. A single-quinta Vintage is the identical legal category under identical rules, but drawn from one named property and normally released in years the house has not declared classically — hence Quinta de Vargellas, Quinta do Bomfim, Quinta do Vesúvio, Quinta do Roriz and Quinta da Cavadinha filling the gaps. It is not a second wine and not a lesser category: it is a Vintage Port from one farm, usually released later and priced lower.
exp: The commercial logic is the point: a house cannot declare every year without devaluing the category, so the single-quinta bottling monetises good but undeclared vintages while protecting the classic name. Vesúvio is the exception that proves the rule — Symington bottles it as a single quinta in almost every vintage.

q: Define Crusted Port and Garrafeira Port, and say who makes each.
accept: crusted is an unfiltered multi vintage blend with three years in bottle garrafeira is single vintage aged in glass demijohns
crusted blends vintages unfiltered while garrafeira ages in demijohn and is made by niepoort
crusted needs three years bottle age garrafeira spends at least eight years in glass
ans: Crusted is a blend of several vintages, bottled young and without filtration, then required to rest a minimum of three years in bottle before release. It throws a crust — hence the name — needs decanting, and carries a bottling date rather than a vintage. It is essentially a British trade invention designed to give Vintage character at a Reserve price, and survives as a house style at Graham's, Dow's, Fonseca and Churchill's. Garrafeira is a rare and legally distinct single-vintage category: three to six years in wood, then a minimum of eight years in large glass demijohns, the bonbonnes, before bottling. The non-porous glass halts oxidative development and produces a nutty, delicate, almost Colheita-like wine with a fine soft deposit. Niepoort is effectively the only house that has kept the category alive.
exp: Both exist to test whether you have read the IVDP's category list rather than a shipper's marketing. Garrafeira is also conceptually interesting: it is the only Port style deliberately matured in a vessel that admits no oxygen, which is precisely why it tastes unlike any cask-aged tawny of comparable age.
